item.title: Buying UK Property as a Non-Resident: Mortgages, Tax and Costs in 2026
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Purchasing UK property as an overseas buyer presents unique challenges, from navigating mortgage options to understanding tax implications. With London transactions taking nearly six months on average to complete in 2026, international investors may need to factor in extended timelines alongside financial considerations.

Mortgage Options for Non-Resident Buyers

Non-UK residents typically find fewer mortgage products available compared to domestic buyers. Many high street lenders restrict their offerings, though specialist providers often cater to international investors. Borrowers might consider:

  • Expat mortgages for UK nationals living abroad
  • International buyer products from private banks
  • Limited company structures for portfolio investors

Lenders generally require larger deposits from non-residents, often starting at 25-30% of the property value. Interest rates may also be higher than standard residential products, reflecting the perceived additional risk.

Tax Considerations for Overseas Investors

UK property purchases trigger several tax obligations that non-residents should understand:

  • Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) with a 2% surcharge for non-resident buyers
  • Capital Gains Tax on property sales, now applying to all non-UK residents
  • Income Tax on rental profits if letting the property
  • Inheritance Tax implications for properties held in personal names

The tax treatment varies depending on the buyer's circumstances and whether the property is held individually or through a company structure. Professional tax advice is often essential for international investors.

Additional Costs and Timeframes

Recent data shows London property transactions averaging 174 days from offer acceptance to completion - significantly longer than other UK regions. Overseas buyers may wish to account for:

  • Currency exchange fluctuations during extended completion periods
  • Additional legal fees for cross-border transactions
  • Potential costs for property management services
  • Higher insurance premiums for unoccupied properties

Working with solicitors experienced in international transactions could help streamline the process and avoid unnecessary delays.

While UK property remains attractive to global investors, the combination of financial, legal and logistical factors means thorough preparation is crucial. Seeking specialist mortgage and legal advice early in the process may help non-resident buyers navigate the complexities of the UK market.

item.title: Double council tax removing second homes in some areas
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Recent government data reveals England has seen a significant reduction in second home ownership, with approximately 20,000 fewer properties classed as secondary residences compared to 2024 figures. The decline appears most pronounced in coastal areas where councils have implemented double council tax charges on second homes, with these locations experiencing both steeper property price drops and faster rental growth than the national average.

Double council tax impact on property markets

Analysis of council tax records and Land Registry data shows second home numbers fell by 9.7% in the year to September 2026 across 30 local authorities charging premium rates, compared to just 2.6% elsewhere in England (excluding London). These same areas have witnessed the most substantial house price corrections since the 2022 market peak, with values declining 6.6% versus a 1.2% dip across other regions.

The effect proves particularly stark in nine council areas where second homes represent over 3% of housing stock. Locations including Cornwall, North Devon, the Isle of Wight and the Isles of Scilly have seen average prices fall 8.8% from their peak - nearly triple the 3.0% decline recorded across the rest of England. This translates to approximately £27,000 off a typical £280,000 property in these sought-after coastal destinations.

Diverging trends for buyers and renters

While prospective purchasers benefit from improved affordability in these areas, tenants face growing pressures. Private rents in the nine highlighted districts have surged 21% since late 2022, only slightly below England's 25% average increase. This rental growth continues despite the cooling sales market, reflecting strong demand for holiday lets and limited long-term rental supply.

The analysis reveals a clear geographical pattern: councils with higher proportions of second homes subject to doubled council tax charges show more pronounced price declines. In areas where fewer than 0.5% of properties attract the premium, values remain 1.1% above 2022 levels. Coastal regions demonstrate particularly marked variations, with prices down 9.2% where 3%+ homes pay double tax, compared to 3.0% falls where under 1.5% do.

North Devon leads the downturn with values 14.0% below peak, followed by other popular second home destinations that saw exceptional pandemic-era price growth now partially reversing. For homeowners in these areas, the changing market dynamics may warrant reviewing property strategies, whilst prospective buyers could find improved purchasing opportunities in previously overheated locations.

item.title: Landlords seek data protection clarity on rental register
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Landlords across England are seeking urgent clarity on data protection measures as the government prepares to launch its new private rented sector register. With the phased rollout beginning on 15th December, the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA) has raised concerns about how sensitive information will be handled and who may access it.

Data Protection Concerns for Landlords

The NRLA has written to the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) requesting confirmation that proper safeguards are in place before landlords are required to submit personal details. Key concerns focus on whether residential addresses and contact information could become publicly accessible, potentially creating security risks for property owners.

Particular attention has been drawn to landlords who may have experienced harassment, threats or domestic abuse. The association argues that inappropriate disclosure of home addresses could have serious consequences for these individuals. The NRLA is calling for publication of a completed Data Protection Impact Assessment before the register goes live.

Calls for Transparency and Safeguards

In its letter to the ICO, the NRLA has requested clear explanations about:

  • How landlord data will be stored and shared
  • Which parties will have access to sensitive information
  • What controls will govern use by letting agents and other authorised users
  • How long personal data will be retained

Ben Beadle, NRLA Chief Executive, stated: "Landlords face an impossible choice between complying with the law and protecting their personal safety if proper safeguards aren't confirmed. The government must clarify these details before expecting anyone to submit sensitive information."

Balancing Transparency With Privacy

While the register aims to improve transparency in the private rental sector, questions remain about how this will be balanced with individual privacy rights. The NRLA has suggested that if adequate protections cannot be guaranteed before December, the government should consider delaying implementation.

Property professionals may wish to monitor developments closely as the December rollout date approaches. The government has yet to respond to the NRLA's requests for clarification, leaving many landlords uncertain about what information they'll need to provide and how it will be protected.

As data-sharing initiatives continue to expand across the property sector, this situation highlights the ongoing challenge of reconciling regulatory transparency with robust personal data protection.

item.title: Huge fine for property firm after hundreds of complaints
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

A property sales firm has been ordered to pay over £277,000 in compensation to customers following an investigation by The Property Ombudsman (TPO). The firm, Let Property, faced nearly 200 complaints related to misrepresented rental income projections and unfair treatment of buyers. This marks the largest repayment of its kind, with average payments exceeding £3,200 per customer.

Let Property, which specialises in buy-to-let properties sold between landlords without evicting tenants, charged customers upfront fees of around £3,000 to reserve properties. However, many deals collapsed after valuations and rental income estimates were found to be misleading. TPO described the firm’s failings as “systemic,” prompting the substantial repayment order.

Customer Complaints and Systemic Issues

TPO’s investigation revealed that Let Property’s practices had caused significant financial harm to customers. Buyers were left out of pocket after deals fell through due to inaccurate information provided by the firm. The watchdog noted that the company’s shortcomings were widespread, affecting numerous transactions.

Let Property acknowledged that some customers had faced difficulties, particularly during completion processes in England. However, the firm disputed the total repayment figure quoted by TPO, stating that it had already paid £187,975 in awards to 63 individuals, including sellers, prospective landlords, and buyers. The company emphasised its commitment to improving services and ensuring fair treatment of customers.

Steps Towards Improvement

In response to the complaints, Let Property stated that it had introduced measures to enhance transparency and customer satisfaction. Since 2025, the firm has provided buyers with independent property condition assessments and pre-checks on rental income and tenancy agreements. Additionally, the company assigned dedicated sales progressors to guide buyers through the completion process, aiming to improve communication and support.

Despite these efforts, Let Property rejected claims of routine communication failures and defended its business model, asserting that it operates with fairness and transparency. The firm’s rapid growth—from one employee in 2022 to 57 last year—has raised questions about its ability to maintain service quality as it expands.

This case serves as a reminder for homeowners and landlords to exercise caution when engaging with property firms. Borrowers might consider seeking independent advice and verifying rental income projections before committing to buy-to-let investments. Whilst Let Property has pledged to address its shortcomings, this incident highlights the importance of due diligence in property transactions.

item.title: Limited companies outgrow individual BTL purchases for first time
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

For the first time on record, limited companies have overtaken individual landlords in buy-to-let property purchases, according to new research. Data from Paragon Bank reveals that 52% of mortgaged buy-to-let acquisitions in the first half of 2026 were made through limited companies – a dramatic shift from just 5% in 2018.

The rise of limited company BTL ownership

The trend towards company ownership has accelerated sharply in recent years. In 2022, limited companies accounted for 19% of purchases, rising to 25% in 2023, 34% in 2024 and 41% in 2025. The value of lending tells a similar story, with company purchases representing 53% of buy-to-let mortgage lending in early 2026 compared to just 6% eight years earlier.

HMRC figures obtained by Paragon through a Freedom of Information request show this pattern extends to property ownership more broadly. Non-individual purchasers now represent 42.1% of higher-rate additional dwelling Stamp Duty transactions, up from 15% in 2016/17. Over this period, transactions involving companies increased by 146%, while those by individuals fell by 41%.

Tax changes driving structural shift

This fundamental restructuring of the buy-to-let market stems largely from tax reforms introduced since 2015. The phased withdrawal of mortgage interest tax relief for individual landlords between 2017 and 2020 removed their ability to deduct finance costs from taxable rental income, replacing it with a basic-rate tax reduction.

The 2026 Budget added further momentum to this trend by announcing an additional four percentage point increase in tax rates on personally held property income from April 2027. With limited companies still able to claim mortgage interest as a business expense, the tax advantages of incorporation have become increasingly compelling.

Louisa Sedgwick, Paragon Bank's mortgages managing director, commented: "Limited company borrowing has moved from the margins to mainstream in under a decade. Government policy has been instrumental in this transformation, with landlords taking a more strategic, long-term approach to their investments."

For those considering buy-to-let investments, these figures highlight the growing importance of understanding different ownership structures. While incorporation brings potential tax benefits, it also involves additional administrative responsibilities and costs. Professional financial advice could help landlords evaluate the most suitable approach for their circumstances.

item.title: London rental competition eases as demand falls 31%
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The London rental market has seen a notable easing in competition, with tenant demand falling significantly in October after the peak summer season. According to recent data from Foxtons, registrations from prospective renters dropped by 31.2% between September and October, while the number of applicants per available property decreased from 20 to 14.

Seasonal Slowdown and Increased Supply

The decline in demand coincided with a slight rise in rental property availability, with new listings up by 2.8% compared to the same period last year. Average weekly rents also dipped by 4.8% month-on-month to £581, though Foxtons suggests this is largely due to seasonal trends rather than a structural market shift.

Year-to-date figures paint a mixed picture. While overall tenant registrations are down 10.4% compared to last year, certain areas like West London saw a 1.5% increase. Central London experienced the most significant decline at 15.3%. Despite lower demand, competition remains elevated, with an average of 17.7 prospective renters per property listing over the past year – 1.5% higher than in 2025.

Regional Variations in Rental Prices

Average rents across London have seen modest annual growth of 0.8%, reaching £589 per week. However, the figures vary considerably by location. Surrey led with a 9% increase, followed by North London at 5.4%. In contrast, East and West London saw declines of 0.9% and 1.8% respectively.

Budget-conscious renters may find some relief, with the average tenant spending 98% of their stated budget. Around 62% secured properties below their original price range, though 32% exceeded their planned expenditure. The typical rental budget now stands at £561 per week, up 1.1% year-on-year.

Sarah Tonkinson of Foxtons noted that while demand has softened in Central London, remaining applicants are offering higher budgets – up 4.1% compared to last year. She emphasised the importance of responsiveness in the current market, suggesting that landlords and agents who act quickly on enquiries could gain a competitive advantage during the quieter winter period.

As the market enters its seasonal lull, renters may find slightly more choice and potentially better negotiating power, particularly outside prime central locations. However, with long-term demand still outstripping supply in many areas, sustained rental growth could return in the new year.

item.title: Knight Frank cuts house price forecast to 1% for next year
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Leading property consultancy Knight Frank has significantly downgraded its UK house price forecasts, pointing to economic uncertainty and higher mortgage costs as key pressures on the market. The firm now expects average prices to rise just 1% in 2027, down from a previous prediction of 3% growth. Meanwhile, its five-year outlook to 2031 has been revised from 20.4% to 14.2%.

What's driving the slowdown?

Several factors are contributing to this more cautious outlook. Mortgage affordability remains stretched with five-year swap rates rising from 3.5% to 4.75% between late September and mid-November. Global geopolitical instability and domestic political uncertainty are also weighing on buyer confidence, according to Knight Frank's analysis.

Tom Bill, head of UK residential research at Knight Frank, noted: "The combination of higher borrowing costs alongside economic and political uncertainties continues to dampen market activity and price growth prospects."

Regional variations emerge

The forecast reveals striking regional disparities. Greater London is anticipated to underperform the national average due to longstanding affordability challenges. Prime central London faces particular headwinds, with prices now expected to fall 3% in 2027 compared to previous expectations of modest growth. The five-year outlook for this premium market segment has been slashed from 16.8% to just 6.5%.

In contrast to the sales market, lettings are projected to see stronger growth. Knight Frank predicts national rents will increase 18.1% over five years, with London rents rising slightly faster at 19.2%. This divergence reflects ongoing rental supply shortages and robust tenant demand across most areas.

What this means for homeowners

While the revised forecasts suggest more modest price growth ahead, Knight Frank's analysis points to market stabilisation rather than significant corrections. The property consultancy emphasises that the eventual trajectory will depend on:

  • The pace at which interest rates decline
  • Broader economic conditions through 2027
  • Any changes to housing policy under new governments

Homeowners considering moves or remortgages might monitor how these forecasts develop alongside Bank of England rate decisions. Those in prime central London areas may wish to pay particular attention to local market conditions given the more negative outlook for this segment.

item.title: Government’s EPC C target under pressure as landlords flag major obstacles
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research suggests England's private rental sector faces significant challenges in meeting the government's proposed energy efficiency targets, with nearly 2.5 million properties currently falling below the required standards. The findings from the TDS Charitable Foundation highlight multiple obstacles including unreliable EPC ratings, skills shortages and financial pressures that could hinder progress towards the 2030 deadline.

Landlords raise concerns over EPC reliability

The government's plan requires all privately rented homes in England to achieve at least an EPC C rating by 2030. However, the research reveals widespread scepticism about the current Energy Performance Certificate system, with many landlords questioning whether the ratings accurately reflect a property's true energy efficiency. Meanwhile, tenant awareness of EPCs remains surprisingly low, with some renters unaware of their property's rating or its significance.

These findings come as the EPC system prepares to take on greater importance in determining whether rental properties meet future legal standards. The TDS Charitable Foundation has called for earlier implementation of planned EPC reforms, currently not due until late 2027, to address these concerns and provide clearer guidance for landlords.

Practical barriers to energy efficiency improvements

Beyond questions about the EPC system itself, landlords report facing several practical challenges in upgrading properties:

  • A shortage of qualified tradespeople to carry out energy efficiency improvements
  • Concerns about the quality of available contractors and workmanship
  • Difficulty accessing clear information about government grants and support schemes
  • Financial pressures from rising improvement costs and potential rent increases

The research found particular confusion around available funding options, with both landlords and tenants struggling to navigate the various schemes and determine which might apply to their circumstances. Some landlords expressed frustration at the complexity of accessing financial support, while tenants worried that upgrade costs might ultimately be passed on through higher rents.

Calls for greater government support

In light of these findings, the TDS Charitable Foundation has urged ministers to consider additional measures to support the sector's transition, including:

  • Earlier implementation of EPC system reforms
  • More accessible financial support packages for landlords
  • Clearer guidance on available grants and funding options
  • Initiatives to address skills shortages in the retrofit sector

With the 2030 deadline approaching, these challenges raise important questions about whether the private rental sector can meet the government's energy efficiency ambitions without significant additional support. Property owners and tenants alike may wish to stay informed about potential changes to EPC requirements and available assistance as the policy develops.

By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research suggests England's private rental sector faces significant challenges in meeting the government's proposed energy efficiency targets, with nearly 2.5 million properties currently falling below the required standards. The findings from the TDS Charitable Foundation highlight multiple obstacles including unreliable EPC ratings, skills shortages and financial pressures that could hinder progress towards the 2030 deadline.

Landlords raise concerns over EPC reliability

The government's plan requires all privately rented homes in England to achieve at least an EPC C rating by 2030. However, the research reveals widespread scepticism about the current Energy Performance Certificate system, with many landlords questioning whether the ratings accurately reflect a property's true energy efficiency. Meanwhile, tenant awareness of EPCs remains surprisingly low, with some renters unaware of their property's rating or its significance.

These findings come as the EPC system prepares to take on greater importance in determining whether rental properties meet future legal standards. The TDS Charitable Foundation has called for earlier implementation of planned EPC reforms, currently not due until late 2027, to address these concerns and provide clearer guidance for landlords.

Practical barriers to energy efficiency improvements

Beyond questions about the EPC system itself, landlords report facing several practical challenges in upgrading properties:

  • A shortage of qualified tradespeople to carry out energy efficiency improvements
  • Concerns about the quality of available contractors and workmanship
  • Difficulty accessing clear information about government grants and support schemes
  • Financial pressures from rising improvement costs and potential rent increases

The research found particular confusion around available funding options, with both landlords and tenants struggling to navigate the various schemes and determine which might apply to their circumstances. Some landlords expressed frustration at the complexity of accessing financial support, while tenants worried that upgrade costs might ultimately be passed on through higher rents.

Calls for greater government support

In light of these findings, the TDS Charitable Foundation has urged ministers to consider additional measures to support the sector's transition, including:

  • Earlier implementation of EPC system reforms
  • More accessible financial support packages for landlords
  • Clearer guidance on available grants and funding options
  • Initiatives to address skills shortages in the retrofit sector

With the 2030 deadline approaching, these challenges raise important questions about whether the private rental sector can meet the government's energy efficiency ambitions without significant additional support. Property owners and tenants alike may wish to stay informed about potential changes to EPC requirements and available assistance as the policy develops.

item.title: London’s super-prime property sales slump as rival global markets surge
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

London's super-prime property market has seen a notable slowdown, with both transaction volumes and values declining in the third quarter of 2026. While the capital maintains its position among global luxury property hubs, recent data suggests buyers are turning their attention to rival markets in Asia and the Middle East.

Quarterly decline in London's luxury market

New research from Knight Frank reveals just 42 London homes sold for over $10m (£7.6m) between July and September 2026, down from 46 transactions in the previous quarter. The value of these deals fell more sharply, dropping 50% from $1.46bn to $722m quarter-on-quarter. Average transaction values nearly halved, falling from $31.7m to $17.2m.

Analysts suggest this reflects a temporary absence of exceptionally high-value deals rather than a fundamental market weakness. Whilst transaction numbers fell 9%, this represents a relatively modest decline compared to the value decrease. London now ranks sixth globally for both transaction numbers and total sales value among prime property markets.

Global super-prime hotspots outperform London

Dubai maintained its position as the world's busiest super-prime market with 86 sales, followed closely by Hong Kong (78) and New York (62). Sydney saw particularly strong growth, more than doubling its transactions to 57 and leapfrogging London in the rankings. Singapore also edged ahead with 44 deals.

Hong Kong surpassed Dubai in total transaction value for the first time since 2022, recording $1.58bn compared to Dubai's $1.57bn. The Asian financial hub saw transactions rise 39% year-on-year, with values up 52%. Meanwhile, Sydney's sales jumped 111% to a record 57 transactions, demonstrating the rapid growth of Australia's luxury market.

Longer-term perspective offers reassurance

Despite the quarterly dip, London's annual figures paint a more positive picture. The capital recorded 184 super-prime transactions in the year to September 2026, up from 173 during the whole of 2025. This suggests the market retains underlying strength despite facing increased competition globally.

Property experts note that London continues to outperform several major US markets, including Los Angeles which recorded just 18 super-prime sales - its lowest quarterly total. The capital's established legal system, cultural attractions and education system help maintain its appeal to international buyers, even as newer markets gain momentum.

While London's super-prime market faces challenges, its historic resilience and unique selling points suggest it may be experiencing a temporary adjustment rather than a sustained decline. Homeowners considering high-value property investments might wish to monitor how global economic conditions continue to reshape the luxury real estate landscape.

item.title: Rayner wants the interest earned from tenancy deposits
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has proposed new measures that would see a portion of interest earned on tenants' deposits redirected to the Treasury, in what could become a significant change for England's private rental sector. Housing Secretary Angela Rayner plans to give her department powers to collect earnings from custodial deposit schemes currently operated by three providers.

How deposit protection schemes currently work

Under existing rules in England, tenants' deposits must be protected in one of three government-approved schemes:

  • The Deposit Protection Service (DPS)
  • Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS)
  • MyDeposits

These schemes hold around £5.5bn in deposits collectively, with approximately half held in custodial arrangements where the scheme retains the deposit and any interest earned. Currently, this interest helps fund the free-to-use service for both landlords and tenants.

Proposed changes to deposit interest

The draft legislation, first reported by The Times, would allow the government to claim a share of this interest income from March 2027. While the exact percentage hasn't been specified, the rules aim to prevent scheme administrators from retaining "excessive" profits beyond what's needed to operate effectively.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) states any revenue generated would be reinvested in tenant-focused programmes within the private rental sector. The proposals also include plans to phase out insured deposit schemes, where landlords currently hold deposits and keep the interest.

With approximately 4.7 million deposits protected across England and Wales, these changes could generate substantial income for the Treasury. However, the plans have drawn criticism from opposition parties, with the shadow housing secretary describing them as another form of "stealth tax".

Tenants and landlords in England may wish to monitor these developments, as the proposals could lead to changes in how deposit protection schemes operate. The government has confirmed it will publish regular updates about revenue collected under the new system once implemented.

item.title: Property sandbox hopes to transform the home buying market
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

A pioneering property data initiative could revolutionise the UK's home buying process by enabling secure information sharing between different sectors of the housing market. The Smart Property Data Trust Framework pilot, involving 49 organisations including conveyancers, lenders and government bodies, has demonstrated how adopting open data standards might streamline property transactions.

How the property sandbox works

The innovative scheme created a controlled digital environment where property professionals could test secure data sharing. Unlike current processes where buyers repeatedly provide the same documents to multiple parties, the sandbox showed how verified information could be safely shared between estate agents, conveyancers, mortgage providers and HM Land Registry. Some participants reported accessing necessary property data in under ten minutes after joining the platform.

This "trust once, reuse many" approach addresses one of the major pain points in property transactions. Currently, homeowners often provide identical documents to different organisations, with each conducting separate verification checks. The sandbox pilot suggests these duplications could be eliminated through secure digital data sharing.

Potential benefits for homebuyers

If implemented nationwide, this system could deliver several advantages:

  • Faster transaction times as information flows seamlessly between parties
  • Reduced paperwork and administrative burdens for home movers
  • Lower risk of transactions falling through due to data discrepancies
  • Potential cost savings across the property chain

The success of the pilot has led to calls for establishing a permanent Smart Property Data scheme, initially on a voluntary basis with potential for future statutory implementation. Over 50 additional organisations have already expressed interest in joining an expanded programme.

Next steps for the property sector

The Digital Property Market Steering Group, responsible for implementing digital elements of government property reforms, is being urged to consider the report's findings. Industry leaders suggest the sandbox model could form the basis of wider market transformation, though challenges around data security standards and interoperability between different systems would need addressing.

Maria Harris of the Open Property Data Association noted: "This initiative demonstrates how adopting common data standards can create genuine information portability across the property sector. Moving away from repetitive verification processes represents an important step towards more efficient property transactions."

While full implementation would require coordinated action across government and industry, the pilot suggests technology could play a key role in modernising the UK's property market. Homeowners considering future moves might watch this space for developments that could make the buying and selling process significantly smoother.

item.title: AI that takes the chasing out of selling property
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Estate agents looking to streamline their workflow may benefit from new AI-powered tools designed to automate time-consuming tasks. Agency Office, a UK-based property software provider, has launched an upgraded version of its cloud CRM system that handles routine follow-ups, client communications and document generation automatically.

Automating the sales process

The updated platform introduces ready-made workflows that manage key stages of property transactions without manual intervention. These include chasing valuation requests, arranging viewings, following up on offers and obtaining vendor approvals. The system automatically logs incoming enquiries, schedules appointments and sends reminders when actions are overdue.

According to the company, many sales fall through not because of competition, but due to simple administrative delays. Common pitfalls include valuation requests left unattended over weekends, viewings without follow-up questions, or offers remaining with vendors for extended periods. The new software aims to address these gaps through systematic automation.

Key features for estate agents

The platform offers several time-saving functions designed to reduce agents' administrative burdens:

  • Automated valuation visit scheduling with instant acknowledgement and follow-up reminders
  • Post-viewing feedback requests to buyers and vendors
  • Offer tracking with vendor decision prompts
  • Template-generated brochures and documents for vendor approval via mobile
  • Integrated e-signature functionality for agreements

Each morning, staff receive a briefing highlighting pending actions, overdue items or stalled transactions. Managers gain full visibility of all deals in progress through a central dashboard.

Enhanced communication tools

The system consolidates client interactions across multiple channels into a single shared inbox. Emails, WhatsApp messages, SMS texts and Facebook Messenger communications all appear in one interface, linked to the relevant property listing and contact. This ensures conversation histories remain with the agency rather than being stored on individual negotiators' devices.

AI-powered suggested replies help agents respond promptly to enquiries. Negotiators can review, edit and approve these automated responses before sending. For valuation visits, agents can dictate notes which the system then uses to generate listings, brochures and agreements automatically.

Larger agencies may particularly benefit from the platform's integration capabilities. Webhooks connect with other business tools, sending notifications for events like new listings or booked viewings. Lead generation features help identify potential clients matching an agency's target markets, then run multi-channel marketing campaigns that automatically pause when recipients respond.

As property technology continues to evolve, such automated solutions may help estate agents focus less on administrative tasks and more on building client relationships. While human expertise remains crucial in negotiations, removing routine follow-ups could potentially help complete more sales efficiently.

item.title: Don’t wait for the EPC deadline warns Beresfords Group
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Landlords across England and Wales may wish to start planning for upcoming Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) requirements well ahead of the 2030 deadline, according to property experts. New regulations will require rental properties to achieve a minimum EPC rating of C for both new and existing tenancies from 1st October 2030, with a £10,000 spending cap per property and potential fines reaching £30,000 for non-compliance.

Why landlords should act now

Property specialists suggest that whilst 2030 might seem distant, early preparation could help landlords avoid last-minute costs and complications. Older properties in particular may require substantial upgrades to meet the new standards, as they often have poorer energy efficiency. Industry estimates indicate about 50% of landlords could be affected by these changes.

Steven Bond of Beresfords Group highlights that original benchmarks for energy assessments are becoming harder to find. This means some properties might have lower EPC ratings than landlords realise, making early assessments particularly valuable. Those with multiple properties might consider reviewing their entire portfolio to budget appropriately for necessary improvements.

Understanding exemptions and costs

The legislation includes exemptions for properties where upgrades would exceed the £10,000 investment limit, but landlords would need to provide evidence to qualify. Common areas that may require improvement include:

  • Insulation upgrades in walls, floors and roofs
  • Window replacements for double or triple glazing
  • Heating system modernisation
  • Renewable energy installations

Specialists recommend that property owners familiarise themselves with potential exemption criteria early, as the application process may require professional assessments and documentation. Those who leave improvements until closer to the deadline could face higher costs due to increased demand for contractors and materials.

For landlords unsure about their properties' current ratings or required upgrades, consulting qualified energy assessors could provide clarity. Many letting agents now offer services to help clients navigate the changing regulations and plan cost-effective routes to compliance.

With significant financial implications at stake, proactive planning appears to be the most sensible approach for landlords preparing for the 2030 EPC changes. Starting the process early could help spread costs over time and prevent rushed decisions as the deadline approaches.

item.title: Soaring rents make buying much cheaper according to Lloyds
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

New research from Lloyds Bank suggests that first-time buyers could be financially better off in the long term by purchasing a property rather than renting. The analysis, which compared the costs of buying versus renting across 12 major UK cities outside London, revealed that homeowners could save thousands of pounds over five years, even after accounting for initial costs like deposits and Stamp Duty.

Monthly Savings and Long-Term Gains

The study found that in seven of the 12 cities analysed, monthly mortgage payments were already lower than average rents. Glasgow topped the list, with homeowners saving £288 per month compared to renters, followed by Newcastle (£187) and Bristol (£139). However, the benefits of homeownership extend beyond monthly savings. With a repayment mortgage, buyers gradually reduce their debt and build equity in their property. Over five years, this equity growth, combined with savings on housing costs, could leave buyers around £11,000 better off, even if house prices remain stagnant.

On a national level, the average first-time buyer property costs £230,000, requiring a 5% deposit of £11,500. While the monthly mortgage payment averages £1,285—£121 less than the average rent of £1,406—the long-term financial advantages are even more significant. Over five years, homeowners could add £15,634 to their home equity while saving £7,260 compared to renting.

Equity Growth and Financial Security

Homeownership also offers greater financial stability over time. According to Lloyds, a buyer starting with a 5% deposit could reduce their mortgage from 95% to around 88% of the property’s value over five years, assuming house prices remain unchanged. This increased equity not only provides a financial cushion but could also open up access to more competitive mortgage deals when remortgaging.

Even in cities where renting appears cheaper on a monthly basis, such as Leeds, the long-term benefits of building equity often outweigh the initial savings. In Leeds, renters pay £53 less per month than homeowners, but the equity accrued over five years still leaves buyers better off overall.

For those considering their first property purchase, the analysis highlights the potential financial advantages of homeownership, including monthly savings, equity growth, and greater financial security. Whilst the upfront costs can be significant, the long-term benefits may make buying a more appealing option than renting.

item.title: Sales price forecasts slashed
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent forecasts from Knight Frank suggest a significant slowdown in UK house price growth, with predictions revised to just 1% by 2027. This adjustment comes alongside expectations of stronger rental growth and subdued performance in prime central London properties. For homeowners and potential buyers, these projections could influence decisions in the coming years.

Revised House Price Growth Outlook

Knight Frank’s updated forecast indicates a notable reduction in house price growth over the next few years. Whilst the UK property market has experienced fluctuations in recent times, the predicted 1% growth by 2027 marks a stark contrast to previous trends. This slowdown could be attributed to various factors, including economic uncertainty, rising interest rates, and changing buyer priorities.

For those considering purchasing a property, the revised outlook may prompt a reassessment of timing and investment strategies. Borrowers might consider locking in competitive mortgage rates now, whilst lenders continue to offer favourable deals. Additionally, homeowners planning to sell may wish to evaluate whether delaying their plans could impact potential returns.

Stronger Rental Growth Expected

In contrast to the subdued house price growth, Knight Frank anticipates a stronger performance in the rental market. Rents are forecast to rise more significantly, driven by high demand and limited supply of rental properties. This trend could present opportunities for landlords or those considering buy-to-let investments.

Prospective landlords might explore the potential benefits of entering the rental market, particularly in areas with high tenant demand. However, it’s essential to factor in the costs associated with property management, maintenance, and potential regulatory changes. For tenants, the rising rents could reinforce the importance of budgeting and exploring alternative housing options.

Prime Central London Market Challenges

The prime central London property market is expected to face continued challenges, with weaker performance predicted in the coming years. Factors such as global economic uncertainty, changes in buyer preferences, and higher transaction costs may contribute to this trend. For investors focusing on this segment, it could be worth reassessing strategies to align with the evolving market conditions.

Whilst prime central London has traditionally been a strong performer, the current forecasts suggest a shift in dynamics. Buyers may wish to explore emerging areas or alternative property types that could offer better growth potential. Similarly, sellers might consider pricing strategies that reflect the changing market realities.

As the UK property market navigates these shifting trends, staying informed and seeking professional advice could help homeowners and investors make well-informed decisions. Whether considering buying, selling, or renting, understanding the latest forecasts is a valuable first step.

item.title: Lack of evidence hampering landlord rent increases
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

New research highlights how procedural mistakes and insufficient documentation are preventing many landlords from securing justified rent increases through tribunal applications. The findings reveal systemic issues affecting property investors seeking fair market valuations for their rental properties.

Evidence gaps undermining tribunal claims

Property tribunals frequently reject rent increase requests due to landlords failing to provide comprehensive supporting evidence. Common shortcomings include:

  • Incomplete comparative market analysis for similar local properties
  • Lack of documented property improvements or renovations
  • Absence of professional valuations from qualified surveyors
  • Failure to demonstrate rising maintenance or mortgage costs

Without this crucial evidence, tribunals often rule that proposed increases lack justification, leaving landlords unable to cover their rising costs.

Procedural errors compounding the problem

The research identified several administrative mistakes that further weaken landlords' cases:

  • Missed deadlines for submission of required documents
  • Incorrectly completed application forms
  • Failure to properly serve notices to tenants within statutory timeframes
  • Lack of proper records documenting communication with tenants

Property investors might consider seeking professional guidance to navigate the complex tribunal process correctly. Many letting agents now offer specialist rent review services that could help avoid these common pitfalls.

Market realities versus tribunal outcomes

Industry analysts note a growing disparity between market rental values and tribunal-approved increases. While local market conditions may justify higher rents, tribunals often approve more modest increases unless landlords present compelling evidence.

Landlords may wish to build comprehensive documentation portfolios well in advance of any rent review process. This could include keeping detailed records of all property investments, maintenance costs, and comparable local rents throughout the tenancy period.

For property investors, understanding these tribunal dynamics has become increasingly important in today's challenging rental market. Thorough preparation and professional support appear crucial for landlords seeking fair rent adjustments that reflect their property's true market value and operating costs.

item.title: Investors go corporate as limited companies dominate
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Recent trends in the UK property market reveal a significant shift towards corporate structures for buy-to-let investments. Limited companies now account for over half of mortgaged purchases in this sector, as landlords adapt to evolving tax regulations and seek more efficient ways to manage their portfolios.

The rise of limited company landlords

Over the past few years, the proportion of buy-to-let properties purchased through limited companies has surged, reaching 52% of mortgaged transactions. This marks a notable change in how landlords approach property investment. The shift comes in response to tax reforms that have altered the financial landscape for individual property investors.

By operating through a limited company, landlords may benefit from different tax treatments compared to personal ownership. For instance, mortgage interest remains fully deductible for companies, whereas individual landlords face restrictions on this relief. Additionally, corporation tax rates are generally lower than higher rates of income tax, potentially making limited companies a more tax-efficient option for some investors.

Tax changes driving the corporate shift

The move towards limited companies reflects broader changes in the property investment environment. Recent tax reforms, including the reduction of mortgage interest tax relief for individual landlords, have prompted many to reconsider their investment strategies. Section 24 of the Finance Act 2015, which phased out full mortgage interest relief for higher-rate taxpayers, has been a key factor in this shift.

Furthermore, landlords may find that operating through a limited company offers greater flexibility when it comes to reinvesting profits or planning for inheritance tax. However, it’s worth noting that this approach also comes with additional responsibilities, such as filing company accounts and complying with corporate regulations.

Considerations for property investors

For those considering restructuring their portfolios, it’s important to weigh the potential benefits against the complexities of running a limited company. Key factors to consider include:

  • The potential tax advantages of corporate ownership
  • The administrative responsibilities involved in running a company
  • The impact on mortgage options, as lenders may have different criteria for limited companies
  • The long-term financial goals of the investor

Seeking professional advice from an accountant or financial adviser could be beneficial for landlords exploring this route. Each investor’s circumstances are unique, and what works for one may not be suitable for another.

As the buy-to-let market continues to evolve, limited companies are playing an increasingly prominent role. Whether this trend will persist remains to be seen, but for now, it highlights the adaptability of property investors in response to changing fiscal landscapes.

item.title: From sourced deals to full-cycle partnerships: why property investors increasingly want a team on the ground
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

UK property investors are increasingly seeking comprehensive local support teams to manage acquisitions, renovations and day-to-day operations, as remote investing becomes more prevalent. This shift reflects growing demand for end-to-end property partnerships rather than simply sourcing deals from afar.

The rise of hands-off property investment

With buy-to-let investors frequently purchasing properties outside their local area, many are opting for full-service partnerships to handle all aspects of the investment cycle. This approach allows landlords to benefit from property ownership without the practical challenges of managing distant assets.

Key services now in demand include:

  • Local market analysis and acquisition sourcing
  • Project management for refurbishments
  • Tenant finding and property management
  • Ongoing maintenance coordination

Why investors value local expertise

Property owners may find several advantages in working with established local partners. Regional specialists typically possess in-depth knowledge of rental demand, achievable rental values and area-specific refurbishment costs that remote investors might struggle to assess accurately.

Local operators can also provide faster response times for maintenance issues and better oversight of renovation works. For investors balancing property portfolios with other commitments, this hands-off approach could prove particularly valuable.

Choosing the right property partnership

Those considering a full-cycle property partnership might wish to evaluate several factors before committing. Reputation and track record should be thoroughly researched, alongside transparent fee structures and clear service level agreements.

Prospective partners should demonstrate:

  • Proven experience in the target location
  • Strong relationships with local contractors
  • Robust systems for financial reporting
  • Positive testimonials from other investors

As the property investment landscape evolves, this model of collaborative local partnerships appears set to grow, offering time-poor investors a way to expand their portfolios while minimising hands-on involvement.

item.title: When one more occupier means you need an HMO licence (and can be fined)
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords renting out properties to multiple tenants need to be aware of the rules surrounding Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs). These properties, where three or more unrelated individuals share living spaces, come with specific licensing requirements. Understanding these regulations is crucial to avoid potential fines and legal complications.

What Defines an HMO?

An HMO is typically a property rented to three or more people who form more than one household. A household can include individuals, couples, or family members, and in some cases, live-in employees such as carers or nannies. In England, properties with five or more occupants from two or more households usually require an HMO licence from the local council. This licence specifies the maximum number of occupants and the property standards that must be met. Smaller HMOs may also need a licence if local authorities have additional licensing schemes in place.

The Importance of Licensing for Landlords

Many landlords aim to avoid licensing by limiting the number of occupants. However, this can be challenging as tenants may bring in friends or relatives to share the property, often without the landlord’s knowledge. For example, tenants might move in a partner or take on unauthorised lodgers to help with rent. Landlords must remain vigilant and conduct regular inspections to ensure occupancy limits are not exceeded. Failing to do so could lead to unintentional breaches of housing laws.

Under section 72(1) of the Housing Act 2004, landlords who manage or control an unlicensed HMO that requires a licence may be committing a housing offence. This applies even if the breach occurs unknowingly. For instance, in a case involving Derby City Council, landlord Mr Sejmir Mehmeti faced legal action after temporarily exceeding the occupancy limit at his property. Although he had previously adhered to the rules, a short period of over-occupation led to penalties, highlighting the importance of strict compliance.

Key Takeaways for Landlords

  • Regularly inspect properties to ensure occupancy limits are not exceeded.
  • Be aware of local licensing schemes, which may apply even to smaller HMOs.
  • Communicate clearly with tenants about the rules regarding additional occupants.
  • Understand that unintentional breaches can still result in legal consequences.

Navigating HMO regulations can be complex, but staying informed and proactive can help landlords avoid costly mistakes. By adhering to licensing requirements and maintaining open communication with tenants, property owners can ensure compliance and protect their investments.
